sections.label: Data volume growth estimate
sections.summary: The International Data Corporation estimates data created in the next three years will exceed total data from the past 30 years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The International Data Corporation estimates that the volume of data that will be created in the next three years will eclipse the total data generated over the past 30 years.

sections.label: Mandatory data breach notification
sections.summary: Clause 13 requires organisations to notify the PDPC of data breaches of significant scale.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: To further strengthen organisations’ accountability, clause 13 introduces a system for mandatory notification to the Personal Data Protection Commission, or PDPC, when a data breach occurs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Under this Clause, organisations must notify the PDPC of data breaches that are of significant scale.

sections.label: New personal data offences
sections.summary: Clause 22 sets out new offences for disclosure, use for gain or harm, and re-identification of anonymised information.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Clause 22 sets out new offences for (a) disclosure of personal data; (b) use of personal data that results in personal gain for the offender or another person, or harm or loss to another person; and (c) re-identification of anonymised information.

sections.label: Increased maximum financial penalty
sections.summary: Clause 24 raises the maximum financial penalty to 10% of annual turnover in Singapore or $1 million, whichever is higher.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Clause 24 increases the maximum financial penalty for breaches of Parts III to VI, and the new Parts VIA and VIB, to 10% of an organisation’s annual turnover in Singapore or $1 million, whichever is higher.

sections.label: Ministerial discretion on penalty commencement
sections.summary: The Bill provides Ministerial discretion to review the penalties' effective date, intended no earlier than one year after the Act commences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The Bill also provides for Ministerial discretion to review the effective date for these penalties to commence and we intend for the revised financial penalty cap to take effect no earlier than one year after the Act comes into force.

sections.label: Maximum financial penalty amounts
sections.summary: Under clause 24, the maximum penalty is 5% of annual turnover in Singapore or $1 million, whichever is higher, and $200,000 for an individual.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Under clause 24, the maximum financial penalty that may be imposed on an organisation is 5% of annual turnover in Singapore or $1 million, whichever is higher, and $200,000 for an individual.

sections.label: Data Portability Obligation introduced
sections.summary: Clause 14 adds a Data Portability Obligation letting individuals request their personal data be sent to another organisation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Clause 14 extends this right by providing for a new Data Portability Obligation, which will enable individuals to request for a copy of their personal data to be transmitted to another organisation.

sections.label: Business improvement purposes allowed
sections.summary: New First and Second Schedules in clauses 31 and 32 state organisations may use personal data for business improvement purposes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The new First and Second Schedules introduced in clauses 31 and 32 make clear that organisations may use personal data for business improvement purposes including: operational efficiency and service improvements; developing or enhancing products or services; and knowing the organisations’ customers.

sections.label: Related corporations data sharing
sections.summary: Part 5 of the new First Schedule in clause 31 allows related corporations to collect and disclose personal data among themselves for the same purposes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Recognising this commercial reality, Part 5 of the new First Schedule in clause 31 allows related corporations to collect and disclose personal data among themselves for the same purposes.

sections.label: Deemed consent by notification
sections.summary: Clause 7 introduces section 15A, allowing organisations to notify customers of a new purpose and give a reasonable opt-out period.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Clause 7 introduces the new section 15A, which expands the consent regime by introducing deemed consent by notification.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Under this provision, organisations may notify their customers of the new purpose and provide a reasonable period for them to opt out.

sections.label: McKinsey study on digitisation
sections.summary: A McKinsey study published in October 2020 found companies digitised 20 to 25 times faster during COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: According to a McKinsey study published in October 2020, companies surveyed across all sectors and regions digitised 20 to 25 times faster during COVID-19.

sections.label: Singapore digital competitiveness ranking
sections.summary: In the IMD World Digital Competitiveness 2020 ranking, Singapore came in second, just behind the US.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: For example, in the IMD World Digital Competitiveness 2020 ranking, Singapore came in second, just behind the US.

sections.label: Singapore innovation hub PDPA amendments
sections.summary: The speaker welcomes PDPA amendments, saying the idea that what works in Singapore works everywhere helps its innovation hub position.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: The idea of "if it works in Singapore, it works everywhere" will be very helpful in strengthening Singapore's position as a regional and global innovation hub.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, I generally welcome the amendments to the PDPA.

sections.label: Personal data for business purposes
sections.summary: The amendment facilitates collection, use or disclosure of personal data for business purposes including enhancing goods or services, operations, personalised services and research and development.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Third, the amendment facilitates the collection, use or disclosure of personal data for a broad range of business purposes such as enhancing goods or services, operational processes, personalised services and research and development.

sections.label: Guidelines, whitelist and Government application
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether upstream guidelines, a whitelist or blacklist could prevent breaches, and whether the relaxation applies to Government and public service.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Again, I say this because I know that enforcement has been enhanced, even individuals can be liable for breaches, but, I am wondering, whether it can be more upstream to provide enough guidelines to have more controls in place to prevent this in the first place.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: I understand that it can be too tedious and time consuming for enterprises to keep applying for Government's approval for every relevant business decision.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: But, might there be a "whitelist" or "blacklist" that clearly articulates the boundaries, the "dos" and "don’ts", for the firms?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Fourth, finally, will the "relaxation" in the collection, use or disclosure of personal data for commercial innovation purposes in this Amendment be applied to the Government and public service?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: If so, what measures are in place to ensure consistency and avoid double standards in terms of data protection policy, standards and enforcement?

sections.label: Smartphone use and scam rise
sections.summary: Most Singaporeans use smartphones for social networking or information, and scammers, impersonators and cyber attacks rose nine folds in three years, with RedMart customer data stolen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Most Singaporeans use their smartphones for social networking or to search for information.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And as a result, the number of scammers, impersonators and cyber attacks has jumped nine folds in the last three years with 672 cases in the first 11 months of 2019, with over half the victims in their 20s to 40s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In fact, just a few days ago, personal information from 1.1 million RedMart customers were stolen from Lazada, an e-commerce platform.

sections.label: SIM card details and PDPA penalties
sections.summary: Local-number scams persist despite compulsory customer details for SIM cards since 2005, and breached organisations may pay 10% of annual Singapore turnover or up to S$1 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, some are actually conducted from local numbers and since 2005, it is compulsory to present customer details to telcos when purchasing both a prepaid and postpaid SIM card.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Now, with the revised Bill when organisations have breached the PDPA Act, they could have to pay a penalty of 10% of their annual Singapore turnover or up to S$1 million dollars, whichever figure is higher.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, I would like to ask, how can we better protect Singaporeans against unsolicited messaging and fraudulent communication from criminal syndicates, especially the elderly who are at risk of such scams.

sections.label: GDPR prohibited data categories
sections.summary: The speaker suggests adopting the European General Data Protection Regulation practice of prohibiting processing of specific data categories unless the individual gives explicit consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Perhaps, we could adopt the practice from the European General Data Protection Regulation or GDPR, where there are specific categories of data in which processing such data is prohibited unless explicit consent is given by the individual.

sections.label: Data portability obligation introduced
sections.summary: The new data portability obligation requires organisations to transmit personal data to another organisation in machine-readable format at the individual's request.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The introduction of the new data portability obligation is a welcome one, where an organisation must at the request of an individual, transmit his or her personal data that is in the organisation's possession or under its control to another organisation in a commonly used machine-readable format.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, while the individual can request for his or her data to be transferred from one organisation to another, individuals themselves do not have the specific right to receive a copy of such data in a machine-readable format before it is ported over.

sections.label: Right to request deletion
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether individuals could be granted the right to request organisations to delete their personal data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Could we perhaps go one step further and that in addition to data portability and access to one's personal data, can the individual be granted the right to request organisations to delete personal data at his or her request?

sections.label: Mandatory data breach notification
sections.summary: The Bill's amendments make it compulsory for all organisations to notify the PDPC and affected individuals of data breaches.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Recent data breaches, which affected 1.1 million Redmart and 2.8 million Eatigo accounts, highlight once again the dangers lurking in the shadows of Internet space and the importance of cybersecurity and remedial procedures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Different organisations have very different attitudes towards data protection.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Therefore, I am very glad that the Bill’s amendments will make it compulsory for all organisations to notify the Personal Data Protection Commission or PDPC and affected individuals of data breaches.

sections.label: Breach notification deadlines
sections.summary: The Bill specifies PDPC must be notified within 72 hours and affected persons without undue delay.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: In addition, the Bill specified that PDPC must be notified within 72 hours and affected persons, without undue delay.

sections.label: Protection from unsolicited messages
sections.summary: The SCA will be updated to protect users from unsolicited messages, particularly bulk commercial texts to instant messaging accounts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The SCA will be updated to protect users from unsolicited messages, particularly bulk commercial texts sent to instant messaging accounts, such as WhatsApp and Facebook Messenger.

sections.label: Risk-based accountability approach
sections.summary: The amendments shift the PDPA towards a risk-based accountability approach, allowing organisations to process personal data without consent under legitimate interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: The amendments to the PDPA to shift towards a risk-based accountability approach is practical and in line with modern economy and global data protection laws.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, organisations may process personal data without the consent of individuals in circumstances classified as "legitimate interests".

sections.label: Breach notification to individuals
sections.summary: Organisations must notify affected individuals when a data breach is likely to cause them significant harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: Organisations will also be required to notify affected individuals if the data breach is likely to result in significant harm to them.

sections.label: Clarifying prescribed number scale
sections.summary: A question asks how the number is obtained if significant scale constitutes the prescribed number.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: If significant scale constitutes prescribed number, can I clarify on how this number is obtained?

sections.label: Unsolicited call complaints to PDPC
sections.summary: Over 46,000 complaints on unsolicited calls and text messages were made to the PDPC since 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: More than 46,000 complaints on unsolicited calls and text messages had been made to the Personal Data Protection Commission or PDPC since 2017.

sections.label: PDPA and GDPR requirements compared
sections.summary: The PDPA covers much of the GDPR, but many GDPR requirements are more stringent than the PDPA's.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The PDPA covers much of the GDPR but there are many requirements in the GDPR that are more stringent than that of the PDPA.

sections.label: Government exempted from PDPA
sections.summary: The PDPA exempts the Government, which has its own data privacy standards in other statutes and manuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Unlike the GDPR, the PDPA specifically exempts the Government from having to comply with it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government has explained that this is because it has its own set of data privacy standards, which are set out in the Public Sector Governance Act or PSGA, the Official Secrets Act or OSA, the Banking Act, the Income Tax Act or ITA, the Statistics Act and the Instruction Manual 8 or IM8, among others.

sections.label: Maximum fines across statutes
sections.summary: Maximum fines for violations of the different statutes range from $1,000 to $250,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, the maximum fines for violations of the different statutes range from $1,000 to $250,000.

sections.label: Civil recourse against Government agencies
sections.summary: A citizen harmed by a Government agency data breach has little civil recourse, while the PDPA grants such recourse against offending organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A citizen who has incurred damages as a result of a data breach by a Government agency has little recourse to pursue civil remedies against that agency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The PDPA, on the other hand, grant such recourse against offending organisations.

sections.label: Harmonising data protection under PDPA
sections.summary: National security exemptions can be written into the PDPA, and the speaker hopes Government agencies will eventually be covered by it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If there is a need to maintain discretion because of national security reasons, these exemptions can be explicitly written into the PDPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I hope the Government can eventually harmonise the data protection clauses in the separate legislations and bring them under the umbrella of the PDPA and make the PDPA apply to Government agencies as well.

sections.label: Mandatory data breach reporting
sections.summary: The Bill requires organisations to report breaches likely to cause significant harm or of significant scale, and to notify affected individuals when harm is likely.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The amendments proposed in the Bill will make mandatory and will require organisations to report data breaches to the Personal Data Protection Commission or PDPC, if such breaches are likely to result in significant harm or impact to individuals, and/or are of a significant scale.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Organisations must also notify affected individuals when a data breach is likely to result in significant harm or impact to them, regardless of the scale of the breach.

sections.label: Higher penalties and personal offences
sections.summary: Irresponsible organisations face a higher financial penalty cap, and the Bill introduces offences for individuals mishandling personal data.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: To signal the importance of organisational compliance and the proper handling of personal data, irresponsible organisations will face a higher financial penalty cap of 10% of annual gross turnover in Singapore or $1 million, and if I heard the Minister correctly, whichever is higher.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The Bill also includes the introduction of offences for the mishandling by individuals of personal data and fines and imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or both.

sections.label: Deemed consent by notification
sections.summary: Organisations relying on new section 15A must conduct risk assessments, and the speaker asks how informed consent is ensured.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: What is required of an organisation if it wishes to rely on this new section 15A to obtain deemed consent by notification is that they need to conduct risk assessments to identify and mitigate adverse effects that the collection, use and disclosure of the personal data may have on individuals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I do support and agree that there are benefits for consumers when organisations use data to innovate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I do, however, have questions on how we ensure that deemed consent by contractual necessity and by notification does not lead to unintended and more importantly, uninformed consent?

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I agree that it should not be prescriptive but there must be measures to ensure that individuals fully understand that they are deemed to have given their consent for the use of their personal data if they do not opt out.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: And I am glad that the Minister, in his speech did say that the individuals can also withdraw consent even after the opt-out period.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: What I am asking for is, ensuring that there is informed consent, not necessarily that we take away deemed consent because, at the end of the day, what is important is consumer trust.

sections.label: Clarifying significant harm definition
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a clearer definition of significant harm in section 26B and questions exemptions from notifying individuals under section 26D.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I shall focus my speech on just a few areas where I would like to pose technical clarifications and suggestions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I suggest that the we could, in section 26B, provide a clearer and more precise definition of "significant harm" to an individual that would warrant notification.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The definition provided in section 26B subsection 2 currently seems rather broad.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Also, on this point, allowing for exemption of organisations by the PDPC from notifying affected individuals of data breaches in the new section 26D is problematic.

sections.label: Scapegoating risk for data offences
sections.summary: New offences for unauthorised mishandling of personal data by individuals, including employees, may lead to scapegoating.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: With new offences for the unauthorised mishandling of personal data by individuals, including employees, there is the possibility that "scapegoating" may happen.

sections.label: Right to be forgotten proposal
sections.summary: The speaker suggests extending PDPA retention limits to align with GDPR Article 17, allowing deletion requests and immediate deletion after consent withdrawal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thirdly, I would like to speak about what has been referred to, in the context of the GDPR, as the "right to be forgotten".

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would suggest further extending the retention limitation obligations in the PDPA to be aligned with Article 17 of the GDPR, where individuals may interface with an organisation to request the deletion of data and where withdrawal of consent may lead to an obligation to immediately delete personal data.

sections.label: Bill's data protection changes
sections.summary: The Bill introduces organisational accountability, mandatory breach reporting, risk assessments, data portability, higher penalties, DNC enforcement and new consent exceptions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: The objective then was to provide a baseline standard for data protection in the private sector.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to introduce, inter alia, the concept of organisational accountability, mandatory data breach reporting to the PDPC, new requirements for organisations to conduct risk assessments, a new data portability obligation to enhance consumer autonomy, a higher financial penalty cap, enhanced enforcement of the Do Not Call provisions and new exceptions and definitions of consent to facilitate the use and movement of data by organisations.

sections.label: Consumer assurance after RedMart breach
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the changes assure consumers, especially after the compromise of 1.1 million RedMart and other e-commerce user accounts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: I hope this set of changes will let consumers be assured in this respect.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: This is especially important, in light of the recent compromise of 1.1 million user accounts of RedMart, Lazada's online grocery store and other e-commerce platforms.

sections.label: Consent, DNC and data portability
sections.summary: Express consent remains required for direct marketing, Spam Control Act and DNC changes protect consumers across platforms, and data portability lets consumers switch providers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Express consent will still be required for organisations to send direct marketing messages and updates to the Spam Control Act and Do Not Call or DNC provisions will allow consumers greater protection from unwanted communications across all direct communication platforms, that is, voice calls, SMSes, instant messaging and emails.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: At the same time, with the new Data Portability obligation, consumers no longer need to worry about being locked-in to a single service provider and can easily switch to new services.

sections.label: Questions on PDPA amendments
sections.summary: The member asks about removing the public agency exclusion, protection for data intermediaries, guidance on new criminal offences, and notes 4,500 complaints last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Second, the proposed amendments seek to remove the exclusion for organisations acting on behalf of public agencies from compliance with the PDPA obligations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Can the Minister elaborate on the impact of this amendment and how organisations, acting as the data intermediaries of public agencies, can be accorded protection in the performance of their tasks?

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Can such organisations reasonably comply with their obligations under the PDPA, given that public agencies, that, the principal, are not subject to the provisions of the PDPA?

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Third, the proposed criminal offences against individuals for the mishandling of personal data have been drafted rather widely.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Would the Minister provide some guidance on when and how these provisions would apply?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It has investigated numerous data breaches and received a record-breaking 4,500 complaints last year.

sections.label: Data breach notification requirement
sections.summary: The Bill requires organisations to notify the Commission and affected individuals of data breaches likely to cause significant harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Bill introduces a requirement for organisations to notify the Commission and affected individuals in certain instances where there is a data breach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: One instance is when the data breach results in, or is likely to result in, significant harm to an affected individual.

sections.label: Avoiding consent in certain cases
sections.summary: The Bill allows organisations to avoid asking for consent in certain cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Bill now allows organisations to avoid asking for consent in certain cases.

sections.label: Rise in breach numbers
sections.summary: The number of breaches rose by 273% in the first quarter compared to the same period last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The number of breaches rose by 273% in the first quarter, compared to the same period last year.

sections.label: Online scam victim's life savings
sections.summary: A young professional met at a Meet the People Session was swindled of her $100,000 life-savings in an online scam.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: They also exploit the desperation of victims during this challenging period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I met Mdm K, a young professional, at my Meet the People Session, or MPS, last week, who fell victim to an online scam and was swindled of her $100,000 life-savings.

sections.label: Amendments target legitimate businesses
sections.summary: The Government's amendments for the PDPA and Spam Control Act will only work on legitimate businesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Government’s amendments for the PDPA and Spam Control Act will only work on legitimate businesses.

sections.label: Data breaches at Lazada and Eatigo
sections.summary: Many Members highlighted data breaches at Lazada and Eatigo affecting millions of accounts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Many Members today have highighted the data breaches at Lazada and Eatigo, affecting millions of accounts.

sections.label: Lazada and Eatigo data breaches
sections.summary: The passage cites the Lazada breach of 1.1 million users and the Eatigo breach of 2.8 million users as examples of how massive breaches can be.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: To use the recent Lazada data breach of 1.1 million users and the Eatigo data breach of 2.8 million users as an example, we have a sense of how massive and widespread such breaches can be.

sections.label: Breach notification and penalties
sections.summary: The amendments set a framework for informing the Commission and individuals about significant or harmful breaches, and stiff financial penalties are needed to deter poor data security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: With the amendments, when there is a breach of significant scale or may cause harm to the individual, there is a framework for these businesses and organisations to assess if both the Commission and the individuals concerned must be informed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Consequently, affected parties can take simple measures like changing their passwords to afford immediate protection to their data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: However, we all agree that any data breach is unacceptable and as such, stiff financial penalties is needed to deter poor handling of data security.

sections.label: DNC registry prohibitions
sections.summary: The DNC prohibits businesses and organisations from sending Instant Messages, SMS and so on to Singapore-based telephone numbers registered with the DNC registry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: The DNC already prohibits businesses and organisations from sending Instant Messages or IMs, SMS and so on, to Singapore-based telephone numbers which have been registered with the DNC registry.

sections.label: Overseas vendors and data disclosure
sections.summary: The passage asks how to ensure overseas vendors do not use disclosed data beyond the original intent when they cannot be held accountable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In addition, if a Singapore-based company then discloses data to its overseas vendors, how do we then ensure that the overseas vendor do not use the data beyond the scope of the original intent, especially when we are then unable to hold them accountable?

sections.label: Accreditation system for consumers
sections.summary: An accreditation system could assure consumers their data is secure with companies meeting or surpassing standards, and forewarn them about companies that do not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Four, potentially, an accreditation system can be used, to give consumers some assurance that their data is secure when dealing with companies that meet, or even surpass, standards, and also to forewarn them to exercise caution when dealing with companies that do not meet these stipulated standards.

sections.label: Level playing field and consumer protection
sections.summary: Singapore needs a level playing field between Singapore and foreign companies, without stifling innovation, while protecting consumers and giving them choice and control over personal data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Given that Singapore is at the forefront of data privacy laws, especially in this region, we need to have a level playing field between Singapore companies and foreign companies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We should not stifle innovation too much but we must do our best to protect consumers from manipulative and exploitative practices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We must give consumers the choice and control over their personal data and how it is used.

sections.label: Data breaches and higher penalties
sections.summary: Citing Grab, Courts and Central Depository breaches, the speaker supports raising financial penalties to 10% of gross annual turnover.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: Recent examples include: (a) a data breach by Grab, where the details of over 21,000 GrabHitch drivers and passengers were leaked due to an update of the mobile app; (b) a marketing email sent out by electronics retailer, Courts unwittingly exposed the personal data of over 76,000 customers, and (c) even the Central Depository, whose staff had mailed dividend cheques to outdated addresses, putting at risk the personal data of over 200 account holders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: Given the potential severity of these continued breaches, I am supportive of the Bill's proposed increase in financial penalties, from the current cap of $1 million to 10% of the organisation's gross annual turnover.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: Creating a strict data protection regime and strengthening our enforcement will also be vital in boosting Singapore's position as the region's premier data hub.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: However, going back to the data breach by Grab that I mentioned earlier, I note that this was Grab's fourth instance in two years, where the company was in breach of the PDPA, and in this latest case, the company was given a fine of $10,000.

sections.label: Assistance for SMEs compliance
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Ministry will assist organisations, especially SMEs, or allow a grace period for new PDPA rules.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: To alleviate these concerns, will the Ministry consider providing some form of assistance to these organisations, especially our SMEs or consider perhaps a grace period for the new regulations, so that companies have a longer runway to plan for their organisation's compliance to the latest PDPA rules?

sections.label: Lazada data breach reminder
sections.summary: The speaker says Lazada's recent data breach affecting 1.1 million users is a timely reminder.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Like what the hon Mr Sharael Taha had said, Lazada's recent data breach affecting 1.1 million users or approximately one-fifth the population of Singapore is a timely reminder.

sections.label: Maximum fine and erasure right
sections.summary: The speaker compares Singapore's maximum fine with Hong Kong, Malaysia and the Philippines, asks for reconsideration, and proposes an explicit right of erasure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The maximum financial penalty that can be meted out is a fine amounting to 10% of the defaulting organisation’s annual turnover in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: For comparison, the contravention of Personal Data Laws in Hong Kong attracts a maximum financial penalty of HKD$1 million; in Malaysiam it is RM$300,000 and in the Philippines, it is PHP$5 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The worry, which has been similarly reflected during the public consultation, is that the maximum fine that can be imposed might be too large compared to worldwide standards, especially in Asia.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Could this disadvantage Singapore as an offshore destination, where MNCs might choose other Asian countries over ours to set up operations?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In light of this, can the Ministry reconsider the maximum financial penalty that it is imposing on defaulting organisations to better align with the standards in neighbouring Asian jurisdictions or competing economies?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Lastly, I propose an explicit recognition of the right for individuals to the erasure of their personal data, for the consideration of the Ministry.

sections.label: Right of erasure autonomy
sections.summary: The provision assigning individuals an explicit right of erasure is described as a step toward greater autonomy over personal data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In furtherance of the amendments’ overall objectives, the imposition of this provision assigning an individual the explicit right of erasure is arguably another step ahead to afford greater autonomy to individuals over their personal data.

sections.label: Government standards versus private sector
sections.summary: The speaker clarifies that the Government believes its standards should be as high as, if not higher than, the private sector's.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: The first point I would like to clarify is Mr Giam's assertion that somehow the Government believes that the standards for Government need to be lower than for the private sector.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: We believe the standards for the Government should be as high, if not, higher than for the private sector.

sections.label: Public data security contact centre
sections.summary: A Government Data Security Contact Centre was established and launched publicly on 30 April this year for concerned members of the public.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Externally, for members of the public that are concerned about their data security, they also have one point of contact – the Government Data Security Contact Centre or GDSCC.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: That was established and launched publicly on 30 April this year.

sections.label: Government personal data policies published
sections.summary: The Government's personal data policies, IM8, were published on 30 April this year.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: On the issue of our Government data policy lacking transparency – Mr Giam referred to it; it is IM8 – the Government's personal data policies were published on 30 April this year.

sections.label: PDPA and PSGA control equivalence
sections.summary: The controls are equivalent between the PDPA and the PSGA.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: The controls are equivalent between the PDPA and the PSGA.

sections.label: Cases of leaked government information
sections.summary: The passage lists cases of civil servants and an HDB officer arrested or fined for leaking confidential government information.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: In April this year, we had a civil servant arrested as a result of leaking COVID-19 case numbers, for accessing a Government COVID-19 database without authorisation to retrieve confidential records and giving that information to a friend.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: A public servant and her husband arrested for wrongful communication of information, which was about the implementation of home-based learning by schools.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: And in December 2017, an HDB officer was fined $2,000 for giving confidential information on HDB resale transaction time and changes to the valuation process to a Straits Times journalist.

sections.label: Reviewing PSGA and other legislation
sections.summary: The PSGA and other legislation will be regularly reviewed to keep them relevant and effective in safeguarding personal data.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: As we are reviewing the PDPA today, we will regularly review the PSGA as well as other legislation to ensure that they remain relevant and effective in safeguarding personal data for both the public and private sectors.

sections.label: Data incidents public versus private
sections.summary: The passage compares data exfiltration and PDPC website incident numbers between the private and public sectors in 2018 and 2019.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: For example, in 2018, in the private sector in Singapore, there were about 13 incidents of exfiltration of data through hacking and in 2019, it was 16 incidents.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: In comparison, in the public sector, we had three in 2018 and zero in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: On PDPC's website, in 2018, there were 2,700 instances in the private sector and 4,500 in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I do not have the exact number, but I know it is at least one if not two orders of magnitude lower for the public sector.

sections.label: Members' support and deemed consent
sections.summary: Eleven Members gave explicit support, and the speaker assumes deemed consent from Mr Leon Perera and Mr Louis Chua.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: To be precise, actually, 11 Members have given explicit support and Mr Leon Perera and Mr Louis Chua, I am assuming, I have their deemed consent since I do not think that there is adverse effect on any individual.

sections.label: Updating consent exceptions and deemed consent
sections.summary: The Bill adds business improvement and legitimate interests exceptions, updates the research exception, and clarifies deemed consent for subcontracting and opt-out notices.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Current exceptions to consent cater for scenarios such as investigations and responding to emergencies.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: We are updating this list by adding business improvement and legitimate interests and updating the research exception for the benefit of consumers and organisations in the digital economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The Bill is also clarifying the deemed consent provision to cover multiple layers of subcontracting when needed to fulfil a contract and to facilitate organisations notifying customers and giving a reasonable period to opt out, before they use data for new purposes.

sections.label: Risk assessments before relying on exceptions
sections.summary: Organisations must conduct a risk assessment before relying on the legitimate interests exception or deemed consent by notification.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Before relying on the legitimate interests exception, organisations have to conduct a risk assessment and be satisfied that the overall benefit outweighs any residual adverse effect to an individual.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: And before relying on deemed consent by notification, organisations must conduct a risk assessment to be sure that there is not likely to be any adverse effect on an individual.

sections.label: PDPC investigations, penalties and enforcement powers
sections.summary: PDPC investigated 185 cases and issued $1.7 million in penalties last year, and the Bill enhances its investigation powers and raises the penalty cap.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Last year, PDPC investigated 185 cases, issued 58 decisions and ordered 39 organisations to pay a total of $1.7 million in financial penalties and that includes the highest financial penalty sums the PDPC imposed in 2019, which were $750,000 and $250,000 on IHiS and SingHealth respctively.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The Bill enhances PDPC’s investigation powers and raises the financial penalty cap, to improve the effectiveness of PDPC’s enforcement.

sections.label: Complaints on unsolicited calls and messages
sections.summary: In 2019, the PDPC received 2,255 complaints on unsolicited calls and text messages and took action against 427 organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: In 2019, the PDPC received 2,255 complaints on unsolicited calls and text messages, and has taken action against 427 organisations.

sections.label: Telcos' plus prefix for overseas calls
sections.summary: IMDA has required all telcos to implement the "+" prefix for incoming overseas calls since April this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: For example, IMDA has required all telcos to implement the "+" prefix for all incoming overseas calls since April this year to help consumers better identify and reject spoof calls.

sections.label: Training numbers since launch
sections.summary: More than 6,200 people have been trained since its launch in July last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Since its launch in July last year, more than 6,200 people have been trained.

sections.label: DPTM recognised organisations
sections.summary: The DPTM was launched last year to recognise organisations with good data protection standards, and 37 organisations have been recognised to-date.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: We launched the DPTM last year to recognise organisations with good data protection standards.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: And to-date, 37 organisations have already been recognised.

sections.label: Maximum financial penalty and effective date
sections.summary: The proposed maximum financial penalty is comparable with the Telecommunications Act and Competition Act, and the revised cap is intended to take effect no earlier than one year after the Act comes into force.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The proposed maximum financial penalty is comparable with other domestic legislation such as the Telecommunications Act and Competition Act and signals that data protection is of that level of importance in the digital economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: As I mentioned earlier, we intend for the revised financial penalty cap to take effect no earlier than one year after the Act comes into force, and the Minister has the discretion under the Act to review the effective date.

sections.label: Numerical threshold for data breach
sections.summary: The Regulations will prescribe a numerical threshold of 500 individuals for a data breach of significant scale, and categories of personal data likely to cause significant harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: I think Mr Leon Perera, Mr Louis Ng and also Mr Shawn Huang had asked about this and I want to tell them that we plan to prescribe in the Regulations, a numerical threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: This is something that has been developed through consultation and it is a numerical threshold of 500 individuals for what constitutes a data breach of a significant scale.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The Regulations will also include categories of personal data which, if compromised in a data breach, will be considered likely to result in significant harm to individuals, such as identity theft or fraud.

sections.label: Defences for teaching and research
sections.summary: Defences in the Act are provided for roles such as teaching and research that may require re-identification of anonymised data.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Additionally, we recognise that roles such as teaching and research may require re-identification of anonymised data and hence we have provided for applicable defences for them in the Act.

sections.label: Removal of Government agents exclusion
sections.summary: The removal of the exclusion for agents of Government makes clear that the PDPA applies to all private sector organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the removal of the exclusion for agents of Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: This makes clear that the PDPA applies to all private sector organisations.

sections.label: Removal of Government agent exclusion
sections.summary: Removing the exclusion for agents of Government provides clarity that private sector organisations face the same PDPA obligations regardless of their customers' sector.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The removal of the exclusion for agents of Government would provide much-needed clarity and certainty that private sector organisations are subject to the same obligations under the PDPA regime, regardless of the sector their customers are in.

sections.label: Aligning penalties across sectors
sections.summary: The amendments align penalties and scope of offences for individuals' egregious mishandling of personal data across public and private sectors.

sentences.speaker: Mr S Iswaran
sentences.text: The amendments further strengthen this by aligning the penalties and scope of offences for individuals’ egregious mishandling of personal data across the public and private sectors.
